newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FOCUS - Czech bank results disappoint, tough road seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Czech bank results disappoint, tough road seen.

text.p: The Czech Republic's two largest banks released disappointing 1996 profit figures on Thursday, prompting analysts to forecast tougher times ahead for both them and for the sector as a whole.

Komercni Banka, the largest commercial bank, said its audited 1996 net profit edged up to 5.24 billion crowns ($180 million), calculated according to international accounting standards, from 5.1 billion in 1995.

Meanwhile Ceska Sporitelna, the largest Czech savings bank, reported a full year net profit of 1.9 billion crowns, after 263 million the previous year when provisioning for risky loans bit heavily into its bottom line.
Analysts said that despite the rise in profits at both banks, they, and the sector as a whole face a tough road ahead.
"I'm a little disappointed by the results, especially at Komercni," Martin Nejedly, a banking analyst at Wood and Company told Reuters.
Komercni, widely seen as one of the strongest banks to emerge from the former East Bloc, has consistently led Czech banks in terms of profits since it was hived off from the central bank in 1990.
But Nejedly said last year's performance shows the bank must increase its operations both domestically and abroad if it is to keep its position.

"It shows that if a large bank such as Komercni wants to play a major role in the region, it needs to expand ... and it is becoming clearer that the ability to generate huge profits in the Czech Republic is not possible anymore," he said.
For Sporitelna, the results were a qualified success, according to Chairman Jaroslav Klapal since the bank got an unqualified audit.

Sporitelna's 1995 gross profit was 9.17 billion crowns but the bank, with the urging of its auditor, assigned 9.13 billion to its reserves covering "classified" loans where recovery is seen as doubtful at best.
The bank has been plagued by bad debts since soon after the 1989 fall of communism. At the time the government put pressure on most Czech banks to lend to a new class of entrepreneurs.

Loans were freely dispensed although few Czech bankers at the time knew how to assess credit risk. Much of the money never came back -- 12 banks have since been placed under central bank administration -- though risk assessment has since been tightened.

But the central bank has been tightening as well, and analysts said that Sporitelna, which is still the dominant player on the interbank money market and holder of the vast majority of Czech deposits, could only sit and watch funds under-perform.

"The tightening of monetary policy, such as the minimum reserve requirements, has hurt a lot of banks. They must keep so much money in non-performing reserves that it can't help but show up on the bottom line," said one London-based analyst.
"The central bank doesn't apear to be in a hurry to loosen its grip, which can only hurt banks again this year," he added.

Analysts said, however, that there were some bright spots in the two banks' books. Both they said, have done a lot to clean up their risky loan portfolios and have become better provisioned against the remaining classified credits.
In the 1996, accounting period Sporitelna said it put aside 4.66 billion crowns for reserves with another 3.1 billion planned for 1997.

"The Komercni results are a little lower than expected in terms of net profit, but...if you look at non-performing loans, the amount declined to 26 percent from 31 percent, which is very good," said Miroslav Nosal of Patria Finance.
Shareholders should also be pleased with the announcing of a rise in dividends for 1996, a reward for their patience.
Klapal said Sporitelna's result opened room for "a higher" dividend than last year's five crowns per share, though he declined to specify what the board's proposal would be.
Komercni Chairman Richard Salzmann said Komercni would increase its dividend by "five or six percent" over 1995, putting it at between 120-125 crowns.
($ = 29.07 Czech Crowns)
